flawed_step: 0013: A bound on an error term of order O(z^{-1}) does not directly imply that its derivative is O(z^{-1}). Step 0011 gives no derivative control (and even writes the upper bound as c/|z^{-1}|=c|z|).
counterexample: Fix ε=3π/4, so the domain is |arg z|<π/4, |z|>1. Let R(z)=e^{-z^2}/z. Since Re(z^2)>0 in this sector, |R(z)|=e^{-Re(z^2)}/|z|≤1/|z|, so R(z)=O(z^{-1}); it also satisfies step 0011 with c=1 because |R(z)|≤1/|z|<|z|. But R'(z)=-e^{-z^2}(2+z^{-2}). For z_n=n exp(i(π/4-1/(2n^2))), n≥2, we have Re(z_n^2)=n^2 sin(1/n^2)<1, and hence |R'(z_n)|≥e^{-1}(2-1/n^2). Therefore |z_n||R'(z_n)|≥n e^{-1}(2-1/n^2)→∞, so R'(z) is not O(z^{-1}).
assessment_summary: The proof is valid through the differentiated identity in step 0007, but the conclusion in step 0013 is unjustified. Differentiating a big-O remainder requires additional analytic estimates; its stated magnitude bound alone is insufficient, as the explicit holomorphic counterexample shows.
